content:
# Sirach Chapter 10 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Sirach 10 (31 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 20

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.1: "educate his people" vs. "educates his people"

**EMET:** "A wise judge will educate his people"
**LOGOS:** "A wise judge educates his people"
**PNEUMA:** "A wise judge shapes his people"
**Issue:** Minor tense/voice difference. PNEUMA's "shapes" is interpretive. Consensus: LOGOS — present tense reads as general truth (gnomic present), appropriate for wisdom sayings.

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.2: "rule of a man of understanding" vs. "good government"

**EMET:** "the rule of a man of understanding will be well ordered"
**LOGOS:** "good government depends on the understanding of its leaders"
**PNEUMA:** "Good leadership comes from understanding"
**Issue:** Greek archōn sunetou = "an understanding ruler." EMET is most literal. LOGOS paraphrases. Consensus: EMET modified: "the rule of a man of understanding is well ordered."

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.3: "undisciplined king" vs. "undisciplined king will ruin" vs. "destroys"

**EMET:** "An undisciplined king will ruin his people"
**LOGOS:** "An undisciplined king brings ruin to his people"
**PNEUMA:** "An undisciplined king destroys his people"
**Issue:** Greek apaideutou basileōs apoleitai ho laos = "the people of an uneducated king will perish." EMET and LOGOS are closest. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.4: "the right man at the right time" vs. "the right person at the right time"

**EMET:** "he will raise up over it the right man at the right time"
**LOGOS:** "he will raise up over it the right person at the right time"
**PNEUMA:** "he places exactly the right person in charge"
**Issue:** Greek anthrōpon = "person/man." Consensus: "the right person at the right time" — gender-neutral is appropriate here.

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.5: "confers honor upon the lawgiver" vs. "confers dignity on the one who makes the law"

**EMET:** "he will confer honor upon the lawgiver"
**LOGOS:** "he confers dignity on the one who makes the law"
**PNEUMA:** "He is the one who gives dignity to those who make the laws"
**Issue:** Greek nomographon = "law-scribe/legislator." "Lawgiver" (EMET) is more concise. "Dignity" (LOGOS) for Greek doxa = "glory." Consensus: "it is he who confers honor on the lawgiver."

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.7: "abominable before the Lord" vs. "hateful before the Lord"

**EMET:** "Arrogance is abominable before the Lord"
**LOGOS:** "Arrogance is hateful before the Lord"
**PNEUMA:** "Arrogance is repulsive to God"
**Issue:** Greek bdelygma = "abomination/detestable thing." "Abominable" (EMET) is most literal; "hateful" (LOGOS) is softer. Consensus: EMET — "abomination/abominable" is the standard translation of bdelygma.

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.8: "insolence" vs. "arrogance"

**EMET:** "injustice and insolence and wealth"
**LOGOS:** "violence, arrogance, and greed"
**PNEUMA:** "violence, pride, and the grasping for wealth"
**Issue:** Greek hyperēphania = "arrogance/pride." LOGOS lists three: violence (adiikia in some mss.), arrogance, greed. EMET has "injustice and insolence and wealth." Text varies. Consensus: LOGOS — three-part list is clearest.

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.9: "dust and ashes" — all agree; "bowels are decaying" vs. "body is decaying"

**EMET:** "even in life the bowels are decaying"
**LOGOS:** "even now in life the body is decaying"
**PNEUMA:** "your body is already decomposing"
**Issue:** Greek ta entos autou = "his insides/bowels." EMET's "bowels" is literal and graphic. LOGOS "body" softens. Consensus: "his insides are already decaying" — preserving the visceral image.

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.10: "a long illness" vs. "a slight illness"

**EMET:** "A long illness mocks the physician"
**LOGOS:** "A slight illness mocks the physician"
**PNEUMA:** "A long illness makes a fool of even the best physician"
**Issue:** Greek mikrothusia = text uncertain. Some read "long illness," others "slight illness." The point is that illness humbles even the most skilled healer. Consensus: "A long illness mocks the physician" — the extended illness image is more ironic.

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.11: "will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms" vs. "becomes the inheritance of maggots"

**EMET:** "he will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms"
**LOGOS:** "he becomes the inheritance of maggots, wild beasts, and worms"
**PNEUMA:** "you become food for worms and maggots"
**Issue:** Greek klēronomiā autou — different manuscript traditions vary here. LOGOS inverts the subject — the man becomes the inheritance rather than inheriting. This reversal is probably Ben Sira's intent (irony: the proud man becomes prey). Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.12: "the beginning of human pride is to forsake the Lord" — all agree

**EMET:** "The beginning of human pride is to forsake the Lord"
**LOGOS:** "The beginning of human pride is to forsake the Lord"
**PNEUMA:** "Where does human pride begin? It begins when a person abandons God"
**Issue:** PNEUMA converts the declaration into a rhetorical question — effective but changes form. Consensus: declarative form preserved. EMET and LOGOS identical.

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.13: "beginning of pride is sin" vs. "pride is the root of sin"

**EMET:** "for the beginning of pride is sin"
**LOGOS:** "For pride is the source of sin"
**PNEUMA:** "Pride is sin's starting point"
**Issue:** Greek hoti archē hyperēphanias = "for the beginning of pride is." The construction is unusual. "Root of sin" (SOPHIA) is an interpretive synthesis. Consensus: "For pride is the beginning of sin."

---

## Disagreement 013 — v.14: "overthrown the thrones" vs. "toppled the thrones"

**EMET:** "The Lord has overthrown the thrones of rulers"
**LOGOS:** "The Lord has toppled the thrones of rulers"
**PNEUMA:** "God has pulled rulers off their thrones"
**Issue:** Greek kathelein thronous = "to take down thrones." LOGOS "toppled" is vivid. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 014 — v.15: "plucked up the roots" vs. "uprooted the proud nations"

**EMET:** "The Lord has plucked up the roots of the nations"
**LOGOS:** "The Lord has uprooted the proud nations"
**PNEUMA:** "God has uprooted proud nations"
**Issue:** Greek exerrizōsen = "uprooted." EMET's "plucked up the roots" inverts the image slightly. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 015 — v.18: "those born of women" vs. "those born of woman"

**EMET:** "those born of women"
**LOGOS:** "those born of women"
**PNEUMA:** "those born of woman"
**Issue:** Greek gennetois gynaikos = "those born of woman." Singular "woman" is more natural in English and echoes Job 14:1. Consensus: "those born of woman."

---

## Disagreement 016 — v.19: rhetorical questions format

**EMET:** "What kind is worthy of honor? Human beings. What kind of human beings? Those who fear the Lord..."
**LOGOS:** "Whose descendants deserve honor? Those who fear the Lord..."
**PNEUMA:** "What kind of person deserves honor? The one who fears the Lord..."
**Issue:** The Greek structure is complex. EMET and PNEUMA ask about "kind"; LOGOS asks about "descendants." The Hebrew Genizah text supports the "kind" reading. Consensus: EMET's structure is most faithful.

---

## Disagreement 017 — v.21: "beginning of his acceptance" vs. "beginning of favor"

**EMET:** "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of his acceptance"
**LOGOS:** "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of favor with him"
**PNEUMA:** "The fear of the Lord is where his acceptance of us begins"
**Issue:** Greek archē proslempseos autou = "beginning of his acceptance." EMET is most literal. Consensus: EMET.

---

## Disagreement 018 — v.25: "free persons" vs. "free citizens"

**EMET:** "Free persons will serve a wise servant"
**LOGOS:** "Free citizens will serve an intelligent servant"
**PNEUMA:** "Free citizens may end up serving a wise slave"
**Issue:** Greek eleutheroi = "free men/persons." LOGOS "citizens" adds civic weight. PNEUMA "slave" for Greek paidariō = "servant/young man." "Slave" is too strong. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 019 — v.28: "honor yourself with humility" vs. "hold yourself in esteem with humility"

**EMET:** "honor yourself with humility"
**LOGOS:** "hold yourself in esteem with humility"
**PNEUMA:** "maintain your dignity — with humility"
**Issue:** Greek doxason tēn psychēn sou = "honor/glorify your soul." EMET's "honor yourself" is most literal. Consensus: "Honor yourself with humility."

---

## Disagreement 020 — v.31: antithetical structure

**EMET:** "One who is honored in poverty, how much more in wealth! And one who is dishonored in wealth, how much more in poverty!"
**LOGOS:** "One honored in poverty — how much more when wealthy! And one dishonored in wealth — how much more when poor!"
**PNEUMA:** "If someone is honored even in poverty, imagine how much more when they have wealth! And if someone is scorned even when rich, imagine how much worse when they are poor!"
**Issue:** Ben Sira uses an a fortiori (kal v'chomer) argument. PNEUMA adds "even" and "imagine" for emphasis. LOGOS is the cleanest. Consensus: LOGOS.

---
